q-132240:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region. 

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & ={x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x$-limits are 
$-2\le x\le 2.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100085/assets/a5d544a1c4c7d0227e464aae92f8b282f716fa41ee57daa1061e77e1898a8a00.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 4}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{x+y}\,dA & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{4}{e}^{x+y}\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

q-37859:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}{\int }_{1/x}^{4x}y\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}[{\int }_{1/x}^{4x}y\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}([\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{1/x}^{4x})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}(8{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}(8{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}})\,dx & ={[\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{2x}]}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{1}{2})-(\frac{1}{3}+1) \\  & =\frac{11}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

q-81355:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2-{x}^{2}}x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2-{x}^{2}}dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x[y]_{{x}^{2}}^{2-{x}^{2}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(2-{x}^{2}-{x}^{2})\,dx \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{3})\,dx & =2{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-132289:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{3}\le y\le x}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{x}x\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{x}x\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{x}x\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x{\int }_{{x}^{3}}^{x}dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x{[\,y\,]}_{{x}^{3}}^{x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(x-{x}^{3})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{4})dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{4})dx & ={[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

q-81778:
Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- We already know the intersection of the line $y=x$ with the line $y=2.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$0\le x\le 2.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100085/assets/92b1eda4ccf9e62e1f7310b1ba9bef5cc6c434755e74196d1829a30f2c4a3c53.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,x\le y\le 2}
$$

So, we can express the integral, as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{8}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{8}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})\,dx & ={[\frac{8x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{12}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}-\frac{4}{3}-0 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

q-122554:
The function $F$ can be expressed in terms of its components $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j,
$$

where

$$
P(x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}},\,Q(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{x-y}.
$$

We first find the domain of each component function. Then, we compute their intersection to find the domain of $F:$

- The function $P(x,y)$ is defined when the expression under the radical is positive. So, to find the domain, we solve the following inequality:

$$
3-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<3.
$$

This defines the region ${D}_{1},$ which is the interior of a circle of radius $\sqrt{3},$ as shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100214/assets/f9c3a22a56839165bfd6c3b05f78ca25053553532063192836d0332d2b070436.png)

- The function $Q(x,y)$ is defined everywhere other than when the denominator vanishes. To find where the denominator vanishes, we set it equal to zero and solve:

$$
x-y=0\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

This defines the region ${D}_{1},$ which is the entire plane ${R}^{2}$ with the line $y=x$ removed:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100214/assets/a1ef93cc90bdd59b922723c2c2aa2bd670b43e416923892c9db53b36ac6b7e57.png)

Finally, the domain $D$ of $F$ is given by ${D}_{1}\cap {D}_{2},$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100214/assets/f70cab5ec58e63e1751faa65b575a20da748b3e8ee90cffac8f1f3b029bbbd79.png)

q-122671:
The function $F$ can be expressed in terms of its components $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j,
$$

where

$$
P(x,y)=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}},\,Q(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We first find the domain of each component function. Then, we compute their intersection to find the domain of $F:$

- The function $P(x,y)$ is defined when the expression under the radical is positive or equal to zero. So, to find the domain, we solve the following inequality:

$$
1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ge 0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.
$$

This defines the region ${D}_{1},$ which is the interior of a circle of radius $1,$ as shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100214/assets/9f5f11a4ca31cb796f5a95a1541aa946e24fd1b7079ab8069e5743d41d92d764.png)

- The function $Q(x,y)$ is defined everywhere other than when the denominator vanishes. To find where the denominator vanishes, we set it equal to zero and solve:

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=y=0.
$$

This defines the region ${D}_{2},$ which is the entire plane ${R}^{2}$ with the origin removed:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100214/assets/5b77ad4e9574e94e6a05eee7680f4b57d0190d40583c37c2097acef958cab7e2.png)

Finally, the domain $D$ of $F$ is given by ${D}_{1}\cap {D}_{2},$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100214/assets/95e8d137f90135de1727451fbc96ddfcc325e9e4461054615c91743a4a9ea54a.png)

First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region. To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100385/assets/85d3faac9a27353a8ea5151b3a32f1065aecb02fd07e0b20727c35de0a7fb216.png)

As a result, we get

D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,{y}^{2}-4\le x\le 4-{y}^{2}}.

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{y}^{2}-4}^{4-{y}^{2}}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}-4}^{4-{y}^{2}}f(x,y)\,dx]dy\end{aligned}
$$

q-132410:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region. Writing $y=2x+4$ and $y=4-x$ in terms of $y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2x+4 & \,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{2}y-2 \\ y=4-x & \,⟹\,x=4-y\end{aligned}
$$

To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100385/assets/da7778322523d0d18a5d5e24af075709958d329fc0053c836fd6637aa912752d.png)

D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 4,\,\frac{1}{2}y-2\le x\le 4-y}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x{e}^{y}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{y/2-2}^{4-y}x{e}^{y}\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

q-132512:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region.

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =2-{y}^{2} \\ 2{y}^{2} & =2 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the line $y=0,$ the $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le 1.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100385/assets/eeadcddee3bc966372613ded9304c723768e9b81cd0299ad14084a94c9348463.png)

$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y+1}}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{2-{y}^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y+1}}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{2-{y}^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y+1}}\,dx]dy\end{aligned}

q-81294:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region. 

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2-{y}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}+y-2 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-y+2y-2 & =0 \\ y(y-1)+2(y-1) & =0 \\ (y+2)(y-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le 1.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100385/assets/4eae7bc6756ef5df750bc98431f9e20c9c23869d5ede7f623e79bf7cbb1785c1.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,y\le x\le 2-{y}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{xy}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-{y}^{2}}\sqrt{xy}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{y}^{2-{y}^{2}}\sqrt{xy}\,dx]dy\end{aligned}
$$

q-132414:
The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{3y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{3y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(\frac{1}{3}(3y)^{3}+(3y){y}^{2})dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(9{y}^{3}+3{y}^{3})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}12{y}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}12{y}^{3}\,dy & ={[3{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =3(3)^{4} \\  & =3(81) \\  & =243\end{aligned}
$$

q-132417:
The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{2y}^{y+1}2xy\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}y[{\int }_{2y}^{y+1}2x\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}y[\,{x}^{2}\,]_{2y}^{y+1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}y((y+1)^{2}-(2y)^{2})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}y({y}^{2}+2y+1-4{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(-3{y}^{3}+2{y}^{2}+y)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(-3{y}^{3}+2{y}^{2}+y)\,dy & ={[-\frac{3}{4}{y}^{4}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =-(-\frac{3}{4}-\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-(-\frac{11}{12}) \\  & =\frac{11}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

q-89550:
Notice that $D$ is a type II region. Since $x\ge 0,$ we obtain the following equations in terms of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4 & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4 & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}} & =\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}} \\ 1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =4-{y}^{2} \\ 4-{y}^{2} & =16-4{y}^{2} \\ 3{y}^{2} & =12 \\ {y}^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the $x$-axis, the $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le 2.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14100385/assets/ec8853d64b58c40935b769745d5adb9ebc5c84b7f9407cc93dff4b809ed64ad5.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\sqrt{1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}}\le x\le \sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}.
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}{x}^{3}\,dA={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}/4}}^{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}\,{x}^{3}\,dx\,dy
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}/4}}^{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}\,{x}^{3}\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}/4}}^{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}\,{x}^{3}\,dx]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\,{[\,\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}\,]}_{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}/4}}^{\sqrt{4-{y}^{2}}}\text{ }dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\,\frac{1}{4}[{(4-{y}^{2})}^{2}-{(1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4})}^{2}]dy \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}\,[(16-8{y}^{2}+{y}^{4})-(1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{16})]dy \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}\,(15-\frac{15}{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{15}{16}{y}^{4})dy \\  & =\frac{15}{4}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}\,(1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{16})dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{15}{4}\,{\int }_{0}^{2}\,(1-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{16})dy & =\frac{15}{4}{[y-\frac{{y}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{y}^{5}}{80}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{15}{4}[(2-\frac{4}{3}+\frac{2}{5})-0] \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$
